summary:
A health system that reads each crewmate’s body and the room they are in, on one timeline.

Astrum is a crew health system that runs on board, with no link to Earth: a desktop hub, an iPhone app for each crewmate and a sensor board in the cabin. It notices a change in a person or a room, shows what that is based on, tells the right people in order, and guides whoever is helping through first-aid steps approved by our medical lead. All three parts are built and running together. Watch the 30-second video, then follow one night in the demo.
details:
On the way to Mars, a message to Earth can take 22 minutes to arrive, and the answer another 22 to come back. If someone on the crew gets sick, the people next to them have to handle it.

The website replays three nights on board, as seen on the hub and on a crewmate's phone: https://astrum.caioagralemos.com

How it works

Astrum has three parts. A hub app runs on one computer on board and keeps everything there, so nothing depends on Earth. Each crewmate's iPhone sends their Apple Health and Apple Watch data to the hub over Wi-Fi, if they allow it. A small sensor board in each cabin sends the room's pressure, temperature, humidity, light, noise and vibration. In the demo the crew is simulated and labelled as such, and the cabin CO2 is NASA's own ISS record, replayed; the board does not measure CO2.

The idea at the centre is to judge each reading against that person's own normal. When something changes, the hub tells people in order: first the crewmate, then the Crew Medical Officer, then everyone. If someone needs help, the hub walks them through the first-aid steps, one at a time.

What we cared about

A tired crew has to trust it at 3 a.m., so small changes never wake anyone. Our medical lead, a medical student, reviewed every emergency step, and the AI on board never writes them; it only explains readings and quotes NASA's health research pages.

In a mental health crisis, the hub tells the crew the person needs someone with them and never shows what they wrote.

A crewmate declares a fire. The hub shows the emergency to everyone on board, opens the steps and sends a message to Earth.

Why it matters

Long missions will need crews that can look after themselves, and so will places on Earth where a doctor is far away, like Antarctic stations or ships at sea. Astrum runs offline on an ordinary computer, so it could run there too.

Watch a night on board in the demo: https://astrum.caioagralemos.com/demo. The hub for Mac and Windows and all the code are at https://github.com/caioagralemos/Astrum

Astrum is not a medical device and does not diagnose or treat.
